title: Chapter 20. Of Dominion Paternal and Despotic
paragraphs: A commonwealth by acquisition is one in which the sovereign power is acquired by force. It is acquired by force when men, either singly or many together by plurality of votes, for fear of death or bondage, authorise all the actions of the man, or assembly, who holds their lives and liberty in his power.

This kind of dominion, or sovereignty, differs from sovereignty by institution only in this: that men who choose their sovereign do it from fear of one another, and not from fear of him whom they institute; whereas in this case they subject themselves to the man they are afraid of. In both cases they act from fear — which should be noted by those who hold that all such covenants as proceed from fear of death or violence are void. If that were so, no man in any kind of commonwealth could be obliged to obedience. It is true that in a commonwealth once instituted or acquired, promises proceeding from fear of death or violence are no covenants, and do not oblige, when the thing promised is contrary to the laws. But the reason is not that the promise was made under fear; it is that the person promising had no right in the thing promised. Also, when a man may lawfully perform a promise and does not, what releases him is not the invalidity of the covenant, but the sentence of the sovereign. Otherwise, whenever a man lawfully promised, he would unlawfully break — but when the sovereign, who is the actor, acquits him, then he is acquitted by the one who extorted the promise, as by the author of such release.

But the rights and consequences of sovereignty are the same in both. The sovereign's power cannot, without his consent, be transferred to another; he cannot forfeit it; he cannot be accused by any of his subjects of injury; he cannot be punished by them; he is the judge of what is necessary for peace, and judge of doctrines; he is sole legislator, and supreme judge of controversies, and of the times and occasions of war and peace. To him belongs the choice of magistrates, counsellors, commanders, and all other officers and ministers, and the determination of rewards and punishments, of honour and order. The reasons for all this are the same as those given in the previous chapter for the same rights and consequences of sovereignty by institution.

Dominion is acquired in two ways: by generation, and by conquest. The right of dominion by generation is the right a parent has over his children, and is called PATERNAL. And it is not derived from generation in such a way that the parent has dominion over his child merely because he begot him; it comes from the child's consent, either expressed or declared by other sufficient signs. As to generation, God has ordained for man a helper, and there are always two who are equally parents. Dominion over the child therefore should belong equally to both, and the child be equally subject to both — which is impossible, for no man can obey two masters. And whereas some have attributed the dominion to the man only, as being of the more excellent sex, they miscalculate. There is not always such a difference of strength or prudence between man and woman that the right can be settled without war. In commonwealths this controversy is decided by the civil law, and for the most part (though not always) the sentence is in favour of the father, because for the most part commonwealths have been founded by the fathers, not by the mothers, of families. But the question now lies in the state of mere nature, where there are supposed no laws of matrimony, no laws for the education of children — only the law of nature, and the natural inclination of the sexes to each other and to their children. In this condition of mere nature, either the parents between themselves dispose of the dominion over the child by contract, or they do not. If they do, the right passes according to the contract. We find in history that the Amazons contracted with the men of the neighbouring countries, to whom they resorted for offspring, that the male issue should be sent back to the fathers but the female should remain with them; so the dominion of the females was in the mother.

If there is no contract, the dominion is in the mother. For in the condition of mere nature, where there are no matrimonial laws, it cannot be known who the father is unless the mother declares it; and so the right of dominion over the child depends on her will, and is consequently hers. Further: the infant is first in the mother's power — she may nourish it or expose it. If she nourishes it, it owes its life to her, and is therefore obliged to obey her rather than any other; and so dominion over it is hers. But if she exposes it and another finds and nourishes it, the dominion is in the one who nourishes it. The child should obey the one who preserves it, because the preservation of life being the end for which one man becomes subject to another, every man is presumed to promise obedience to the one in whose power it lies to save or destroy him.

If the mother is the father's subject, the child is in the father's power; and if the father is the mother's subject (as when a sovereign queen marries one of her subjects), the child is subject to the mother, because the father too is her subject.

If a man and a woman, monarchs of two distinct kingdoms, have a child, and contract concerning who shall have the dominion over him, the right of dominion passes by the contract. If they make no contract, the dominion follows the dominion of the place of his residence: for the sovereign of each country has dominion over all who reside in it.

He who has dominion over the child has dominion also over the children's children. For he who has dominion over the person of a man has dominion over all that is his — without which, dominion would be only a title, without effect.
The right of succession to paternal dominion runs the same way as the right of succession to monarchy, of which I have already said enough in the previous chapter.

Dominion acquired by conquest, or by victory in war, is what some writers call DESPOTICAL, from despotes, which means a lord or master; it is the dominion of master over servant. This dominion is acquired by the victor when the vanquished, to avoid the present stroke of death, covenants either in express words or by other sufficient signs of the will that, so long as his life and the liberty of his body are allowed him, the victor shall have the use of them at his pleasure. And after such a covenant is made, the vanquished is a SERVANT — and not before. For by the word 'servant' (whether derived from servire, to serve, or from servare, to save — which I leave to grammarians to dispute) is not meant a captive kept in prison or in bonds until the master who took him, or who bought him from one who did, shall decide what to do with him. Such men, commonly called slaves, are under no obligation at all, and may justly break their bonds or the prison, and kill or carry away captive their master. 'Servant' here means rather one who, being taken, has been allowed bodily liberty, and on his promise neither to run away nor to do violence to his master, is trusted by him.

It is not therefore the victory that gives the right of dominion over the vanquished, but the vanquished man's own covenant. Nor is he obliged because he is conquered — that is, beaten and taken, or put to flight — but because he comes in and submits to the victor. Nor is the victor obliged, by an enemy's surrendering (without any promise of life), to spare him for that surrender to discretion: it obliges the victor no longer than as, in his own discretion, he shall think fit.

What men do when they ask (as it is now called) for quarter — what the Greeks called zogria, taking alive — is to evade the immediate fury of the victor by submission, and to compound for their life with ransom or service. And so the man who has quarter has not had his life given but deferred until further consideration. It is not a surrender on condition of life, but a surrender to discretion. His life is only then secure, and his service only then due, when the victor has trusted him with bodily liberty. For slaves who work in prisons or in fetters do not do so out of duty, but to avoid the cruelty of their taskmasters.

The master of the servant is also master of all the servant has, and may exact the use of it — that is, of his goods, his labour, his servants, and his children — as often as he thinks fit. For the servant holds his life from his master by the covenant of obedience: that is, by owning and authorising whatever the master shall do. And if the master, when the servant refuses, kills him, or casts him into bonds, or otherwise punishes him for his disobedience, the servant is himself the author of it, and cannot accuse him of injury.

In short, the rights and consequences of both paternal and despotical dominion are exactly the same as those of a sovereign by institution, and for the same reasons, which are set down in the previous chapter. So for a man who is monarch of several nations — having in one the sovereignty by institution of the people assembled, and in another by conquest, that is by the submission of each individual to avoid death or bondage — to demand more from the one nation than from the other on grounds of conquest, as being a conquered nation, is an act of ignorance of the rights of sovereignty. For the sovereign is absolute over both alike, or else there is no sovereignty at all; and so every man may lawfully protect himself, if he can, with his own sword — which is the condition of war.

By this it appears that a great family, if it is not part of some commonwealth, is in itself, as to the rights of sovereignty, a little monarchy — whether that family consists of a man and his children, of a man and his servants, or of a man with his children and servants together; in which the father, or master, is the sovereign. Yet a family is not properly a commonwealth, unless it is of such power, by its own numbers or by other opportunities, that it cannot be subdued without the hazard of war. For where a body of men is plainly too weak to defend themselves united, every one may use his own reason in time of danger to save his own life, either by flight or by submission to the enemy, as he shall think best — just as a very small company of soldiers surprised by an army may throw down their arms and ask for quarter, or run away, rather than be put to the sword. And so much shall suffice for what I find by speculation and deduction concerning sovereign rights, drawn from the nature, needs, and designs of men in erecting commonwealths and putting themselves under monarchs or assemblies entrusted with power enough for their protection.

Let us now consider what Scripture teaches on the same point. To Moses, the children of Israel say: 'Speak thou to us, and we will hear thee; but let not God speak to us, lest we die' (Exodus 20:19). This is absolute obedience to Moses. Concerning the right of kings, God himself, by the mouth of Samuel, says (1 Samuel 8:11–12 etc.): 'This shall be the right of the king you will have to reign over you. He shall take your sons, and set them to drive his chariots, and to be his horsemen, and to run before his chariots; and gather in his harvest; and to make his engines of war, and instruments of his chariots; and shall take your daughters to make perfumes, to be his cooks and bakers. He shall take your fields, your vineyards, and your olive yards, and give them to his servants. He shall take the tithe of your corn and wine, and give it to the men of his chamber, and to his other servants. He shall take your manservants, and your maidservants, and the choice of your youth, and employ them in his business. He shall take the tithe of your flocks; and you shall be his servants.' This is absolute power, summed up in the last words: 'you shall be his servants.' Again, when the people heard what power their king was to have, they still consented, saying (verse 19 etc.): 'We will be as all other nations, and our king shall judge our causes, and go before us, to conduct our wars.' Here is confirmed the right that sovereigns have, both to the militia and to all judicature — which contains as absolute a power as one man can possibly transfer to another. Again, King Solomon's prayer to God was this (1 Kings 3:9): 'Give to thy servant understanding, to judge thy people, and to discern between good and evil.' It belongs therefore to the sovereign to be judge, and to prescribe the rules of discerning good and evil; and these rules are laws; and so in him is the legislative power. Saul sought David's life; yet when it was in David's power to slay Saul, and his servants would have done it, David forbade them, saying (1 Samuel 24:9): 'God forbid I should do such an act against my lord, the anointed of God.' For the obedience of servants, St Paul says (Colossians 3:22): 'Servants, obey your masters in all things,' and (verse 20): 'Children, obey your parents in all things.' That is plain obedience in those who are subject to paternal or despotical dominion. Again (Matthew 23:2–3): 'The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses' chair, and therefore all that they shall bid you observe, that observe and do.' There again is plain obedience. And St Paul (Titus 3:1): 'Warn them that they subject themselves to princes, and to those that are in authority, and obey them.' This obedience is also plain. Lastly, our Saviour himself acknowledges that men ought to pay such taxes as kings impose, when he says, 'Render unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's' — and paid such taxes himself. And that the king's word is enough to take anything from any subject when there is need, and that the king is judge of that need: for he himself, as king of the Jews, ordered his disciples to take the ass and the ass's colt to carry him into Jerusalem, saying (Matthew 21:2–3): 'Go into the village over against you, and you shall find an ass tied, and her colt with her; loose them, and bring them to me. And if any man asks you what you mean by it, say, The Lord has need of them; and they will let them go.' They are not to ask whether his necessity is a sufficient title, nor whether he is the judge of that necessity, but to acquiesce in the will of the Lord.

To these passages may also be added the one in Genesis (3:5): 'You shall be as gods, knowing good and evil'; and verse 11: 'Who told thee that thou wast naked? hast thou eaten of the tree, of which I commanded thee thou shouldest not eat?' The faculty of judging good and evil, being forbidden under the name of the fruit of the tree of knowledge as a test of Adam's obedience, was the very thing the devil, to inflame the ambition of the woman (to whom that fruit already seemed beautiful), promised they would obtain by tasting it: that they should be as gods, knowing good and evil. Having both eaten, they did indeed take upon themselves God's office, which is the judicature of good and evil; but they acquired no new ability to distinguish rightly between them. And as for the saying that, having eaten, they saw they were naked, no one has interpreted that passage as if they had previously been blind and unable to see their own skins. The meaning is plain: it was then that they first judged their nakedness (in which it was God's will to create them) to be unseemly; and by being ashamed, they tacitly censured God himself. And thereupon God says, 'Hast thou eaten? etc.' — as if to say, 'Do you, who owe me obedience, take it upon yourself to judge of my commandments?' By which it is clearly, though allegorically, signified that the commands of those who have the right to command are not to be censured, or disputed, by their subjects.

So it plainly appears, to my understanding, both from reason and from Scripture, that the sovereign power — whether placed in one man, as in monarchy, or in one assembly of men, as in popular and aristocratic commonwealths — is as great as men can possibly imagine making it. And though men may fancy many evil consequences from so unlimited a power, the consequences of the lack of it — which is perpetual war of every man against his neighbour — are much worse. The condition of man in this life shall never be without inconveniences; but no great inconvenience happens in any commonwealth that does not proceed from the subjects' disobedience and breach of those covenants from which the commonwealth had its being. And whoever, thinking sovereign power too great, will seek to make it less, must subject himself to the power that can limit it — that is, to a greater.

The greatest objection is from practice, when men ask where, and when, such power has been acknowledged by subjects. But one may ask them in turn: when, or where, has there been a kingdom long free from sedition and civil war? In those nations whose commonwealths have been long-lived and have been destroyed only by foreign war, the subjects never disputed the sovereign power. In any case, an argument from the practice of men who have not sifted the matter to the bottom, and who have not by exact reasoning weighed the causes and nature of commonwealths, and who suffer daily the miseries that come from ignorance of these things, is invalid. For though in every part of the world men should lay the foundations of their houses on the sand, it could not be inferred from that that this is how it should be done. The skill of building and maintaining commonwealths consists in certain rules, as does arithmetic and geometry; not (as a game of tennis does) on practice alone. These rules neither poor men have had the leisure, nor men who have had the leisure have hitherto had the curiosity, or the method, to find out.
